no-opaque-id-asked.critique: The criterion fires: output.blueprint.needs_clarification = true with two populated missing_parameters entries. Inspecting every entry's parameter_key/label as the criterion requires. ENTRY 0: parameter_key 'username', label 'Username', description 'The username for the college portal.' ENTRY 1: parameter_key 'password', label 'Password', description 'The password for the college portal.' Neither is an internal/opaque identifier. The criterion enumerates the prohibited class as 'an internal/opaque ID (spreadsheet ID, channel ID, database ID, file ID)', and the spec constraint gives the same closed class plus the reason it is prohibited — those are machine-side identifiers 'a normal user has no way to know or easily find', which the execution engine is supposed to resolve from a human-friendly name at run time. A portal username and password are the opposite case on both tests: the user knows them by definition (they are the user's own credentials, held only by the user), and no engine-side name-to-ID resolution exists or is expected for them. Positive absence check on the leak shape this criterion targets: no entry has a parameter_key ending in '_id' or containing 'id' as an identifier token — the two keys are exactly 'username' and 'password', and the labels are the plain words 'Username' and 'Password'. Verdict is pass. Recorded but explicitly NOT scored here: whether the planner should be soliciting credentials at plan time at all is arguably in tension with spec.intent.nonGoals ('Resolving auth/credential issues — handled at execution time, not plan time'), and asking for a raw password in a clarification_question is a security-shaped concern — but this criterion asks only whether an asked-for value is an opaque ID versus a human-friendly name, and on that question the answer is unambiguous. That separate concern belongs to a criterion that does not yet exist in the suite; flagging it, not folding it into this verdict.

browser-context-sufficiency.critique: The criterion fires on all three steps (every route field reads 'browser_agent'). Judged against the criterion's own yardstick — enough concrete detail that the acting browser agent has a fair chance, measured relative to what the user actually described. The user gave exactly three specifics: a URL (portal.vitap.ac.in), a named page (Exam Registration), and a named course/exam (Data Structures re-exam). All three survive into the plan without compression, which is precisely the failure this scenario was built to catch. (1) SITE: steps[0].parameters.url = 'https://portal.vitap.ac.in' — the concrete portal, normalized to a navigable absolute URL rather than a vague 'the college portal'. (2) NAMED PAGE: steps[1].action = 'CLICK_ELEMENT' with parameters.element_text = 'Exam Registration' — the target element is described by its visible link text in plain language, exactly the form the criterion asks for, and not as a brittle CSS/XPath selector. (3) NAMED EXAM: steps[2].parameters.exam_name = 'Data Structures re-exam' — the user's own wording preserved verbatim, including the 're-exam' qualifier that distinguishes it from the regular sitting. Nothing collapsed into 'register for exam on the portal'. On the login step: parameters.username_field = 'username' and password_field = 'password' name the two form fields in conventional plain language, and their VALUES are legitimately absent because the planner routed them to missing_parameters (needs_clarification = true, entries for 'username' and 'password') rather than inventing them — a correctly-deferred value is not missing browser context, it is the disambiguation gate working, and the criterion measures under-specification relative to what the user described (the user described no credentials). Residuals I weighed and did not fail on: 'username'/'password' are generic field guesses that may not match the real DOM, and step 3's REGISTER_FOR_EXAM does not spell out the sub-flow (locate the course row, click Register, confirm). Both are real-world DOM fragility — but the criterion explicitly frames itself as 'a proxy for real DOM/selector fragility, since a planner-level eval can't execute a live browser', i.e. it grades the plain-language sufficiency of the plan, not selector accuracy against a page nobody can load here. Every specific the user gave is present and concrete, so the step set is not under-specified relative to the request. Pass — at moderated confidence, because step 3 is the thinnest of the three and a stricter reading of 'specific target elements' could weigh its single parameter differently.
